Analysis by Richard Cowan 

English speaking Canada covers a vast area, but only has about 20 million inhabitants. (There are almost 10 million francophones, mostly in Quebec.) Most of its people live within 100 miles of the US border, and get a steady diet of US television and pop-culture, so it is easy for a visiting American to underestimate how different it is. It would appear that the current Conservative (minority) government – under Prime Minister Stephen Harper – is making the same error, or they are the last American wannabes. 

Nowhere is this confusion more embarrassingly obvious than in its love for the Drug War, especially on marijuana. While most Canadians are very concerned about maintaining their sovereignty and national identity against their problematic neighbor, and polite anti-Americanism colors much of its culture and politics, the current government is trying to be more prohibitionist than the US. Nowhere is this more bizarre in the government’s handling of the Marc Emery, Michelle Rainey, Greg Williams case. 

See 

Marc Emery Forced to Accept Plea Bargain for Five Years in A Canadian Prison. Charges Against Co-Defendants to Be Dropped. Canada Betrays Its Citizens and Its Sovereignty.

 

Just when we thought it could not get any weirder… it did. As the above link reported, a deal was almost worked out that would have sent Emery to prison for five years, but at the last minute it was vetoed by Ottawa. So today, The National Post, Canada’s excellent conservative national newspaper once again editorialized against sending Emery to the US. "Marc Emery should not be extradited." 

The National Post has also called for the full legalization of marijuana, as have other major Canadian papers with conservative editorial pages. (See what I mean about Canada being different?) 

Although the National Post is anti-prohibitionist, it allows government officials to have their say. I only have a problem with this when papers then parrot the prohibitionist party line, which the NP does not. In keeping with that practice, earlier this month, the NP published an Op-Ed by Tony Clement, the hopelessly ignorant Health Minister, “The cost of getting high ” 

Here are a few excerpts that deal with cannabis: 

“The UN Office of Drugs and Crime reports that Canada now has the highest proportion of marijuana users in the industrialized world at 16.8% for those between 15 and 64 years of age…” 

He even wrongly claimed that “Eight percent of youth report using marijuana daily.”

One might think that these numbers would indicate that prohibition is counterproductive. After all, The Netherlands has a rate of marijuana use by teens that is less than half Canada’s actual rate, but he seems to have missed that point. 

See 

International “Prohibition Situation Report” – DEAland Media Ignore News Showing Cannabis Prohibition Is Counterproductive. Coffee Shop System Survives. Ironically, Prime Minister Harper is not above learning the wrong lessons from other countries. Shortly after he became Prime Minister he suggested that Canada might learn about keeping Canada’s English and French communities united by studying the success of Belgium! (The French and Dutch parts of Belgium are constantly at loggerheads, and the country may yet split in two.) 

Other than Harper, Canadians tend to follow European news more closely than do most Americans, so he was ridiculed. Alas, he did not try to learn anything from Belgium’s neighbor to the north. 

Clement also said, “The most recent Canadian Addictions survey indicates that while youth alcohol-use rates have stayed relatively consistent since 1989, use of marijuana by youth has almost doubled in the same period…” and although he doesn’t mention it, tobacco use went down, as it did in the US… without arresting anyone for using it. See 

T’was Another Great Victory. Teen Marijuana Use Down; Oxy Use Up. Teen Cigarette Use Went Down More Than Teen Marijuana Use. 

and 

“Teens See Marijuana As Less Harmful Than Cigarettes.” Oh, The Horror! Is Health Canada Dangerous to the Health of Canada’s Teens? 

Drugs often described as "recreational" are illegal for a reason: They take a terrible toll on human health. 

A single marijuana joint may cause as much lung damage as up to 20 tobacco cigarettes, and regular use can cause respiratory problems such as recurring bronchitis…

See 

British Lung Foundation Cons Media. Blaming Cannabis for Problems Caused By Prohibition. Tripping Over the Party Line. The Media Fell For It, As Usual, But UK Anti-Tobacco Group Does Not. 

And Paul Armentano has dealt with this nonsense very well on Alternet. 

Adding insult to injury, or threat of injury by state violence, Clement then goes on to say, or rather lie, “We will provide youth with the plain truth on the harms of illicit drug use: There are no "safe" amounts, and there are no "safe" illicit drugs.” 

We will highlight the fact that for young people, having impaired judgment is a safety issue… 

We think it's time young people were told the plain truth about the real cost of getting high.”

Inasmuch as Canada has a halfhearted, or perhaps I should say half-assed and hardhearted, medical cannabis program, this statement is truly bizarre. 

See 

Canadian Court Slaps Health Canada’s Arbitrary Limit On Patient Choice of Growers. Years of Harassing Sick and Dying. Bureaucratic Arrogance. 

Consequently, it is informative to look at the actual health costs of “substance abuse” in the province. The Center for Addictions Research of BC’s website offers some insight. 

“According to a recent study of hospital discharge data for diseases or conditions linked to substance use, in 2005 there were 

27,622 hospitalizations related to tobacco, 

14,790 hospitalizations related to alcohol, and 

4,817 hospitalizations related to illicit drugs. 

A comparison of these findings reveals that hospitalizations for illness related to tobacco and alcohol are much higher than those for illicit drugs. In fact, illnesses attributable to tobacco and alcohol are five and three times, respectively, more common than those attributable to illicit drugs. 

Between 2001 and 2005, hospitalization rates for illnesses related to substance use steadily increased. During this same time period, deaths attributed solely to alcohol increased while deaths due solely to illicit drugs decreased.” 

As for dollar costs: 

“Total costs for substance-related harms are estimated at $6.058 billion (or $1,463 per BC resident) per year. About 75% of the total burden is related to harms from tobacco and alcohol: 

tobacco $2.331 billion (38%) 

alcohol $2.219 billion (37%) 

illicit drugs $1.508 billion (25%)” 

Keep in mind that British Columbia has one of the highest rates of marijuana use in Canada, despite increased levels of police harassment outside of Vancouver proper, but very little of these costs are directly related to cannabis. 

From 1999,

see 

The Reality Of the Marijuana Situation In Canada: Unequal Injustice. Alcohol Costs Canadian Health Almost 100 Times As Much As Marijuana.Tobacco: Almost 200 As Much – Article and Editorial 

But none of this matters to the Harper government. They are merely an extension of the Canadian police, and even the National Post and the majority of the Canadian population that supports the full legalization of cannabis are too “nice” to confront the threat to their freedom and sovereignty. One other difference between Canada and the US is that there is really no national marijuana reform movement there. The battle for our freedom is being fought by others. Good on them, and shame on us.

See 

Wake Up Canada! 2006 Canadian Professional Police Association Political Agenda. “Prime Minister of Canada to Open the CPPA Annual Legislative Conference”
